extract:
Eric Clapton was born on March 30, 1945, in Ripley, Surrey, England, and emerged in the early 1960s as part of the British blues boom that congregated around London clubs like the Marquee and the Crawdaddy. Steeped from his teenage years in the recordings of Robert Johnson, Muddy Waters, Freddie King, and B.B. King, he became the defining guitarist of that scene, valorized to the point that the famous "Clapton is God" graffiti appeared on a Islington wall in 1967. His active recording career stretches from 1963 to the present, making him one of the longest-running figures in rock and blues.

Clapton first drew attention with The Yardbirds, joining in 1963 and playing on early sides like "For Your Love" before quitting in 1965 over the band's pop direction. He then joined John Mayall's Bluesbreakers, whose 1966 album Blues Breakers with Eric Clapton, recorded with a Gibson Les Paul through a Marshall combo, set a new template for British blues guitar tone. That same year he formed Cream with Jack Bruce and Ginger Baker, a power trio whose albums Fresh Cream, Disraeli Gears, Wheels of Fire, and Goodbye produced standards like "Sunshine of Your Love," "White Room," and "Crossroads." After Cream's dissolution he made one album with Blind Faith alongside Steve Winwood and Baker in 1969.

The next phase saw Clapton retreat from guitar-hero status into a more song-oriented role. Touring and recording with Delaney & Bonnie reshaped his approach, and his self-titled 1970 solo debut featured their band. He then formed Derek and the Dominos with Bobby Whitlock, Carl Radle, and Jim Gordon, joined in the studio by Duane Allman, for Layla and Other Assorted Love Songs, produced by Tom Dowd at Criteria Studios in Miami. Heroin addiction sidelined him for much of the early 1970s, but he returned with 1974's 461 Ocean Boulevard, which yielded a chart-topping cover of Bob Marley's "I Shot the Sheriff" and steered him toward a relaxed, roots-driven sound on follow-ups like Slowhand (1977), home to "Wonderful Tonight" and "Cocaine."

Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, Clapton recorded for RSO, Warner Bros., Reprise, and Duck Records, working with producers including Phil Collins (Behind the Sun, August) and Russ Titelman. His commercial peak came with Unplugged (1992), which won six Grammys and recast "Layla" as an acoustic shuffle, and with "Tears in Heaven," written after the death of his young son Conor. He returned explicitly to the blues on From the Cradle (1994) and the B.B. King collaboration Riding with the King (2000), and paid tribute to his hero on Me and Mr. Johnson (2004).

Clapton remains one of the few artists inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame three times, for the Yardbirds, Cream, and his solo work. He founded the Crossroads Centre in Antigua to treat addiction and stages the recurring Crossroads Guitar Festival to fund it. In recent years he has continued to tour selectively and release records such as Old Sock and the Christmas album Happy Xmas, while drawing controversy for outspoken statements on COVID-19 vaccines. His legacy as a conduit between American blues and mainstream rock guitar remains foundational, even as critical opinion of his later output and public persona has grown more divided.
title: Eric Clapton
